lead: Access control answers one question for every request: may this subject perform this operation on this object? A subject is a user or process. An object is a file, folder, device or record. An operation is read, write, execute or delete. The answer comes from a model, such as an access matrix, and a policy enforced by the operating system or an application. It exists so data and services reach only the right people. Banks use it for accounts, hospitals for records, and Linux and Windows for files.
prereq: You need: 6.5 Operating system security: UNIX and Windows for users, processes and file permissions.

blocks.text: An access matrix is a table. Rows are subjects: users or processes that request access. Columns are objects: files, folders, devices or records. Each cell lists the rights, also called operations, that the subject holds on the object. Common rights are r for read, w for write, x for execute and - for none. In the figure, Bob has rw on f2 and Carol has rwx on f3. The matrix is a model; real systems store it in one of two ways.

An access control list (ACL) stores one column per object. The ACL for f2 is: Alice r, Bob rw, Carol r. A capability stores one row per subject. Bob's capability list is: f1 r, f2 rw, f3 x. An ACL is checked when a subject opens an object. A capability is presented by the subject when it requests an object.

Linux file ACLs use setfacl to add entries and getfacl to test them. setfacl -m u:alice:rw f1 gives Alice read and write on f1. getfacl f1 prints the ACL. setfacl -m d:u:bob:r dir1 sets a default ACL for new files in dir1.

In discretionary access control (DAC), the owner of an object decides who gets access. UNIX permissions are DAC. In mandatory access control (MAC), the system decides using labels. Every subject gets a clearance level and every object gets a classification level. A label is a security level such as public, secret or top secret. The user cannot change the label.

Bell-LaPadula protects confidentiality with two rules. No read up: a subject cannot read an object with a higher classification than its clearance. No write down: a subject cannot write to an object with a lower classification. The second rule stops a secret being copied into a public file.

Biba protects integrity and reverses the directions. No read down: a subject cannot read an object with lower integrity, so low-quality data does not contaminate a high-integrity process. No write up: a subject cannot write to an object with higher integrity. Read the names carefully: Bell-LaPadula is about secrecy, Biba is about trustworthiness.

Role-based access control (RBAC) gives permissions to roles, not directly to users. A role is a job function such as cashier, auditor or nurse. Users are assigned to roles. A session is a login in which a user activates some roles. Permissions are operations on objects. RBAC scales because a new cashier gets the cashier role, not twenty separate file rights.

Separation of duties (SoD) stops one person from completing a sensitive task alone. Static SoD says a user cannot hold two conflicting roles, such as buyer and payment approver. Dynamic SoD says the same user cannot activate both roles in one session.

Attribute-based access control (ABAC) decides from attributes. A subject attribute is department or clearance. A resource attribute is owner or classification. An action attribute is read or approve. An environment attribute is time or network. A policy might allow read when subject.department equals resource.department and time is before 18:00. ABAC is flexible but needs clean attribute data.

A policy is a rule. Enforcement is the check made on every request. A policy decision point (PDP) computes allow or deny. A policy enforcement point (PEP) blocks or passes the request. A reference monitor is the abstract guard that checks every access, cannot be bypassed, and is small enough to verify.

Least privilege gives a subject only the rights needed for its task, for the shortest time. Privilege creep is the slow growth of rights when people change jobs and old rights are not removed. Review rights on a schedule and remove unused entries.
FAR = FA ÷ N_impostor, FRR = FR ÷ N_genuine
blocks.where: FAR is the false acceptance rate; FA is the number of impostor attempts accepted; N_impostor is the total impostor attempts; FRR is the false rejection rate; FR is the number of genuine attempts rejected; N_genuine is the total genuine attempts.

blocks.text: Biometric access control uses a fingerprint, face or iris. It is taught in only a few courses. FAR measures how often a wrong person is accepted. FRR measures how often the right person is rejected. A strict threshold lowers FAR and raises FRR.

figure.caption: Read the f2 column downwards and you get f2's access control list: Alice r, Bob rw, Carol r, three entries kept with the file. Read Bob's row across and you get his capability list: f1 r, f2 rw, f3 x, three entries kept with the user.

spec.title: Access matrix
spec.aria: An access matrix with subject rows Alice, Bob and Carol against object columns f1, f2 and f3. The f2 column is highlighted: Alice r, Bob rw, Carol r, which is the ACL of f2. Bob's row reads f1 r, f2 rw, f3 x, which is his capability list.

examples.question: An access matrix has subjects Alice, Bob, Carol and objects f1, f2, f3. Alice has rw on f1 and r on f2. Bob has r on f1, rw on f2 and x on f3. Carol has r on f2 and rwx on f3. (a) Can Bob write f2? (b) Can Carol read f1? (c) Give an ACL for f2. (d) Give a capability list for Bob.
steps: Read the row for Bob and the column for f2. The cell is rw. It contains w, so Bob can write f2. Encode yes as 1.
Read Carol row, f1 column. The cell is -. It has no r, so Carol cannot read f1. Encode no as 0.
ACL for f2 is the f2 column. Entries: Alice r, Bob rw, Carol r. Count = 3.
Capability list for Bob is the Bob row. Entries: f1 r, f2 rw, f3 x. Count = 3.
examples.answer: Bob can write f2; Carol cannot read f1; the ACL for f2 has 3 entries; Bob's capability list has 3 entries.
examples.check:
matrix = {
    'Alice': {'f1': 'rw', 'f2': 'r', 'f3': '-'},
    'Bob': {'f1': 'r', 'f2': 'rw', 'f3': 'x'},
    'Carol': {'f1': '-', 'f2': 'r', 'f3': 'rwx'},
}
bob_write_f2 = 1 if 'w' in matrix['Bob']['f2'] else 0
carol_read_f1 = 1 if 'r' in matrix['Carol']['f1'] else 0
acl_f2 = [s for s in matrix if matrix[s]['f2'] != '-']
bob_caps = [o for o in matrix['Bob'] if matrix['Bob'][o] != '-']
print(bob_write_f2)
print(carol_read_f1)
print(len(acl_f2))
print(len(bob_caps))

traps: An ACL sits with the object; a capability sits with the subject. Do not swap them in a diagram.
MAC checks labels and clearances, not a user name. A root account may still bypass some checks in a real system, but that is not the model.
Bell-LaPadula is confidentiality: no read up, no write down. Biba is integrity: no read down, no write up.
An RBAC role is a job function with permissions and sessions. A UNIX group is only a container for users; it is not a role model by itself.
False acceptance and false rejection move in opposite directions when the biometric threshold changes.

quiz.q: Define subject, object and operation in access control.
quiz.a: A subject is a user or process that requests access. An object is a resource such as a file or record. An operation is an action such as read, write or execute.

quiz.q: Why store an ACL per object?
quiz.a: Opening a file needs a quick check of who may use this file. An ACL groups the entries by object, so the check reads one list.

quiz.q: Using the figure, can Alice execute f3? Can Bob read f3?
quiz.a: Alice f3 is -, so no execute. Bob f3 is x, so no read; Bob has execute only.

quiz.q: Give the ACL for f3 from the figure.
quiz.a: Alice none, Bob x, Carol rwx. The ACL can omit Alice or list her with -.

quiz.q: Why does Bell-LaPadula no write down block a Trojan leaking a secret?
quiz.a: A secret process cannot write to a public object. The copied secret cannot leave the secret level, so the leak is blocked.

quiz.q: How is RBAC different from a UNIX group?
quiz.a: A group collects users for file permissions. RBAC gives permissions to job roles, supports sessions, and can enforce separation of duties.

quiz.q: There are 1000 impostor attempts and 5 are accepted. There are 800 genuine attempts and 8 are rejected. Find FAR and FRR.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry is moving from static roles to policy engines that combine RBAC and ABAC, often called policy-based access control. Zero trust treats every request as untrusted and checks identity, device and context each time. Cloud identity and access management applies the same matrix idea to APIs, buckets and virtual machines. Search terms: NIST zero trust architecture, policy decision point, attribute-based access control, identity governance and privilege creep.
